If you have no experience with cigars, this serves as your one-stop-shop to learn all the basics.

The absolute basics

Before you enter the delicious cigar smoking hobby you should learn a few key basics. Cigars come in all sorts of shapes and sizes, referred to as vitola. For your first cigar I recommend sticking to coronas or smaller (robustos or petite coronas would be ideal). In this post, and in this subverse in general, I’ll only be referring to premium cigars.

Cigars span an extremely wide range of prices from <$1USD to > $1,000USD. As a first timer (or even more beginners/amateurs/non-advanced smokers), I’d recommend staying in the $4-$8 range. Anything much more than that and you probably won’t be able to pick up on the subtleties that makes the cigar worth the extra cost.

What should I smoke?

Before you smoke your first cigar, you need to choose one. For your first cigar, stick to a smaller cigar that has mild strength. (Strength refers to the nicotine content). Smoking a strong cigar without any tolerance built up is a sure-fire way to experience nicotine sickness and I promise you it’s not fun. Here are some beginner, easy to find recommendations:

  • Don’t be shy about asking your tobacconist for recommendations. It’s their job and they’re usually pretty knowledgeable (especially for recommending beginner cigars)

  • Arturo Fuente Hemingway Short Story (honestly, you can’t go wrong with most <$8 Fuentes as a beginner

  • Perdomo Champagne

  • Flor de las Antillas (an introduction to a little spice)

  • Perla del Mar (might be difficult to find, is part of the Arturo Fuente family)

  • Avo Classic

  • Drew Estate Undercrown (if you think you might like a darker leafed cigar)

  • Padron x000 series

  • If a cigar has any signs of mold on it, just pick a different one

How do I smoke my cigar?

  • Do NOT inhale. Ever.

  • Cutting - Cut just a tiny bit off the cap of the cigar to allow air to flow through the cigar. Here’s an example of the perfect cut from Neptune’s website

  • Toasting - To toast it, just put a flame up to the foot of the cigar and rotate the cigar to give the foot an even burn. This is an investment to make sure your cigar burns evenly throughout. Try to not to burn the cigar – the actual flame shouldn’t really touch the cigar.

  • Lighting - Without letting the flame touch the cigar, hold the flame near the foot and slowly and deeply draw with your mouth to get the cigar lit. Rotate the cigar while lighting to ensure an even light. Note: Anything with butane is fine. Lighters with lighter fluid (most Zippos) are considered bad because of the odor. Matches/bic lighters are totally fine.

  • Smoking

    • Never inhale. You’ll get sick.

    • Never smoke on an empty stomach. You’ll get sick.

    • If you begin to feel ill, just stop smoking and eat/drink something sugary. No shame – it’s happened to every smoker.

    • Ideally, you should take 1 puff every minute (too fast it gets hot & too slow it goes out). A slow, long draw is better than fast, quick puffs because it helps keep the tobacco cooler.

    • Don’t ash too much; it makes the tobacco burn hotter. Let the ash build. I usually let it build about an inch before I ash (so it doesn’t fall on my lap).

    • Don’t extinguish the cigar when you’re finished. It smells awful and is widely regarded as poor etiquette. When you’re finished, just put the cigar in the ashtray and let it die an honorable death on its own.

How to store my cigars?

Cigars must be stored within certain temperature and relative humidity ranges. Cigars are typically stored in spanish cedar humidors with a humidification system. The industry standard is 70F at 70%RH. (There are many debates on the ideal storage environment, but we won’t get into those here since this is for beginners). Prolonged storage outside the 70/70 range will negatively impact your cigars. Too hot? Beetles are possible. Too dry? Loss of delicious oils & harsh smoke. Too humid? Mold. (“But what about plume?”…that’s not a beginner discussion, more info to follow).

Have no fear, proper cigar storage is a lot easier than it sounds. I very, very, very, very, very (see how many times I wrote “very”) highly recommend beginning your storage with Tupperware, lovingly referred to as a Tupperdor. Cigar tupperdors are rapidly increasing in popularity due their low cost, high functionality, and low maintenance. Just buy some kitchen Tupperware (I use these), wash and dry it, throw one or two 69% Boveda packs in it, and keep it out of direct sunlight. Done. You’re good for at least a few months.

Now go enjoy a cigar and let us know about your experience!

"Censorship" is a very loaded term, and it's a lazy way to describe such a nuanced topic. I suggest you read what he says more closely and understand his reasoning. For those who haven't been following the block size debate closely, I'll try to summarize:

  1. Virtually everyone agrees that the 1MB block size limit will need to be increased at some point. The big questions are 'when' and 'how'. As for 'when', one side thinks the block size should be increased as soon as possible before the network becomes overloaded, while the other side thinks that the urgency is being overstated. The 'how' revolves around how much the block size limit should be increased, whether there's a way to do it without a risky hard fork, and so on.

  2. Since the debate has gone on for quite some time, people on both sides generally acknowledge there still isn't any consensus on the matter. Therefore, those who feel the issue is urgent have decided to try and forgo the consensus process by deploying code which is programmed to increase the block limit on the condition that 750 of the last 1000 blocks were mined using the alternate implementation BitcoinXT.

  3. Theymos has determined that due to the fact that the consensus process has not been completed, implementations containing code to modify the consensus rules by which Bitcoin operates are not considered to be 'Bitcoin', but an alternate currency altogether, and are therefore off-topic. Read more about contentious hard forks and why they're bad on Bitcoin.org.

Given that Bitcoin operates on rules which have achieved near-absolute consensus, and that BitcoinXT contains code which could cause a hardfork without the required consensus, I agree with Theymos and others who state that BitcoinXT is an altcoin which poses a risk to the Bitcoin network. Treating BitcoinXT as off-topic until A.) a hardfork actually reaches consensus, or B.) the hardfork code is removed, is absolutely the right decision for maintaining a unified Bitcoin ecosystem. I understand that many of us want to increase the block size limit, but I don't believe most people advocating BitcoinXT understand the risk of catastrophic consensus failure where incompatible blockchains exist simultaneously. The whole point of operating the network on consensus rules is to avoid damaging the existing network and infrastructure. The necessity of reaching consensus on serious issues like hardforks is not debatable.
